The core challenge is managing concurrent access to shared mutable state while avoiding both safety violations (like race conditions) and liveness failures (like starvation). The transition from coarse-grained locking (barriers, mutexes) to optimistic concurrency control (atomic transactions) reflects a fundamental trade-off between simplicity and efficiency. In high-frequency trading, for instance, a race condition could lead to double-spending, while convoy starvation might cause a proprietary algorithm to miss optimal execution windows. Middleware systems must provide strong isolation guarantees to prevent attackers from exploiting timing channels, as discussed in Section 4.10. The mathematical structure involves partially ordered sets of events (happens-before relations) and formal verification using temporal logic to ensure invariants hold across all possible schedules. Practical considerations include lock-free data structures that use CAS instructions to avoid blocking, which ties directly to the non-blocking techniques covered in Section 4.9. The empirical telemetry includes metrics like cache coherence misses, TLB shoot-waits, and scheduler preemptions, which correlate with synchronization overhead.
